content.title: About
content.content: A muffin is a small, cake‑like baked good made from a blend of rye flour, wheat flour, eggs, milk, and a modest amount of sugar. The English version is known for its denser crumb and the distinctive rye aroma, often complemented by a slight tang from a sourdough starter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rye muffins appeared in England in the 19th century as a quick snack for laborers.
Traditionally they were served with butter or jam, but modern recipes frequently add dried fruit or nuts.
Rye flour gives the muffin a darker color and a characteristic earthy flavor that sets it apart from wheat‑based versions.
In some English regions the muffin is called a “sourdough bun,” highlighting the use of a fermented dough.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Rye flour contains more fiber than wheat, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The rye component causes a slower rise in blood sugar, beneficial for glycemic control.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Rye contributes a modest amount of iron, supporting blood formation.

items.title: Moderate protein content
items.content: The muffin offers plant‑based protein that can help meet daily needs.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Both rye and wheat flours contain gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Even small servings can be calorie‑rich due to butter and sugar.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes include salt, which should be considered by those limiting sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and spread with butter, jam, or cream cheese. They pair well with hot tea or coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 2 months).
